Growing as a designer

E-commerce platform for merchants | 7,600+ employees

E-commerce platform for merchants | 7,600+ employees

E-commerce platform for merchants | 7,600+ employees

summary

Growing as a designer

In a moment when the tools, the skills, and the expectations for designers are all changing at once, how do you build a career in design?

When Shopify’s CEO Tobi Lütke published a memo in April 2025 saying AI usage was no longer optional, it read from the outside like an ultimatum. Inside Shopify's design team, however, VP of Design Katarina Batina says it simply confirmed what many were already feeling: the way they worked was about to change.

The team was given broad access to AI tools and tokens, along with time to experiment. Since then, more designers have started shipping code themselves, and the distance between prototype and product has narrowed. Roughly 60% of Shopify’s designers now push code to production (a 38% increase since last September), and the team has built more than 5,500 prototype sites on Quick, Shopify’s internal hosting platform. As a result, a coded prototype built by a designer collaborating with River, Shopify’s Slack-based coding agent, is no longer just a static reference for engineering. Quite often, it becomes the final experience itself.

And when the way design gets done changes this rapidly, the trajectory to career growth has to shift too. The traditional path of mastering a singular craft and gradually expanding your scope is no longer the only way to evolve. This case study follows Shopify designers across disciplines as they rethink their workflows, learn new tools, and navigate the uncomfortable, exciting space of being beginners again.

Katarina Batina and Staff Motion Designer Yaël Bienenstock

Growing as a designer

In a moment when the tools, the skills, and the expectations for designers are all changing at once, how do you build a career in design?

When Shopify’s CEO Tobi Lütke published a memo in April 2025 saying AI usage was no longer optional, it read from the outside like an ultimatum. Inside Shopify's design team, however, VP of Design Katarina Batina says it simply confirmed what many were already feeling: the way they worked was about to change.

The team was given broad access to AI tools and tokens, along with time to experiment. Since then, more designers have started shipping code themselves, and the distance between prototype and product has narrowed. Roughly 60% of Shopify’s designers now push code to production (a 38% increase since last September), and the team has built more than 5,500 prototype sites on Quick, Shopify’s internal hosting platform. As a result, a coded prototype built by a designer collaborating with River, Shopify’s Slack-based coding agent, is no longer just a static reference for engineering. Quite often, it becomes the final experience itself.

And when the way design gets done changes this rapidly, the trajectory to career growth has to shift too. The traditional path of mastering a singular craft and gradually expanding your scope is no longer the only way to evolve. This case study follows Shopify designers across disciplines as they rethink their workflows, learn new tools, and navigate the uncomfortable, exciting space of being beginners again.

Katarina Batina and Staff Motion Designer Yaël Bienenstock

This era will really belong to the people who are most generative and whose creative ambition keeps moving as high as the tools will allow them.

Katarina Batina

VP of Design, Shopify

This era will really belong to the people who are most generative and whose creative ambition keeps moving as high as the tools will allow them.

Katarina Batina

VP of Design, Shopify

This era will really belong to the people who are most generative and whose creative ambition keeps moving as high as the tools will allow them.

Katarina Batina

VP of Design, Shopify

KEY INSIGHTS

What we learned

01

Designers have more leverage than ever

Product building used to have tidy lanes: design owned desirability, engineering solved feasibility, and product drove viability. Today, those boundaries have faded. With access to new tools, designers at Shopify are now able to own the problems they are trying to solve with direct access to customer data and insights and can quickly move to prototyping potential solutions directly in production. This shift gives designers massive leverage to scale their impact and shape the product. As Katarina puts it: “It’s never been easier to hop on and start contributing to code, even if you’re not technical.”

02

Try everything and keep moving

With so many AI tools available, which ones are worth learning? Katarina’s advice is simple: try everything. No one has years of experience working this way yet. A designer with fifteen years of experience is figuring this out alongside someone who graduated last spring. “You will make quantum leaps if you take the time to actually learn these new tools,” she says. It’s also reflective of how Shopify operates: questioning existing processes and being willing to rethink how work gets done. But Katarina also cautions against losing sight of the problem you’re trying to solve and the people you’re building for by over-focusing on AI, especially when the conversation around what’s new vs outdated seems to change by the day.

03

Growth happens through real work

One of the defining moments in Katarina’s career came during a 2012 internship at Facebook. Despite having little experience designing software, she found herself in critiques alongside some of the industry’s best designers. "That three-month internship changed the entire trajectory of my career,” she says. “I credit that experience so much with where I am today and I'm in a position now where I can hopefully extend the same kind of opportunity.”

Enter: Shopify’s Design Apprenticeship Program (DAP). The six-month program embeds a small group of junior designers on product and brand design teams, where they’re paired with mentors and work on real, shipped products. Its driving philosophy is that designers grow fastest when they’re surrounded by experienced designers and trusted with meaningful work.

in action

Creating a vision that's hard to ignore

When Luke Dupont came back from the holidays in January, he noticed that everyone around him was building. “I got really scared because I wasn’t,” he says. “I was still just doing the thing that I’m really good at, which is Figma.” So he took the opportunity to dive in.

His demo revisits an idea he first explored months earlier: rethinking how a merchant’s online store could be built inside Shop. The first version was a Figma prototype, but it never went far. “It felt very static and very not real,” he says.

This time, he went straight to a coded prototype. In an afternoon, he built a working version using real merchant data and Shop's existing components: a store where every section could be rearranged, rebuilt for different shoppers, or generated from a prompt. Instead of turning it into a deck, he shared the prototype through a Quick link, so anyone could open it and watch it change as he worked. The link went up the chain. By Monday, Luke had a team and a real project.

I’ve been having more fun in my career than I have in years. Just having this new way to fully unlock and to build the thing, not just draw it.

Luke Dupont

Principal Product Designer, Shopify

in action

Meeting engineering more than halfway

Across Shopify, designers are getting closer to code. Design Apprentices Pearl Sequeira and Taylor Cottrell are two strong examples.

Pearl recently redesigned how the Shop app collects and displays buyer reviews. She started her exploration in Figma, then built the experience inside the app using Claude Code and Codex. “It helps us make decisions really fast, cut things that don't work, and double down on things that are beginning to look good,” she says. While she still uses Figma to map out a direction, she now turns to code to test the motion and interactions that are difficult to communicate with a static mock.

Taylor approached a similar problem from the other direction. Before opening Figma to design a new feed card, he dropped an old engineering spec into an AI assistant to quickly map out the technical constraints. The tool surfaced details like latency, lazy loading, and deduplication before he drew a single screen. Because of this groundwork, his subsequent conversations with engineers started from a shared understanding.

Engineers felt that I had gone more than halfway across the table to understand what they were dealing with. It made them more open to the stuff we ended up presenting.

Taylor Cottrell

Design Apprentice, Shopify

in action

One character, six tools

For much of her career, the things motion designer Yaël Bienenstock pushed for “would often just get watered down more and more as we got to the end of the project.” Motion was often the last thing on the timeline, squeezed into the nice-to-have category. Now, she can build them herself.

Her demo features a floating character she created for the design team's website, whose jacket transforms with every click. She modeled the character after a colleague using Krea, then jumped from tool to tool for the rest: Midjourney for the outfits, Gemini to fine-tune them, Rive for pinpoint edits on specific details, stills stitched into generated video, composited and timed in After Effects, then into Claude in the terminal for a working prototype an engineer could take to the finish line.

That creative freedom goes beyond work. With thousands of outfit photos in her camera roll, but no easy way to find them, Yaël built an app in her free time that turns mirror selfies into 3D avatars for cataloging her outfits, complete with animated icons and shaders.

You might not have a perfect output, and that's totally fine. Knowing that this is not where it ends—that was a huge unlock for me.

Yaël Bienenstock

Staff Motion Designer, Shopify

Designers have more leverage than ever

Product building used to have tidy lanes: design owned desirability, engineering solved feasibility, and product drove viability. Today, those boundaries have faded. With access to new tools, designers at Shopify are now able to own the problems they are trying to solve with direct access to customer data and insights and can quickly move to prototyping potential solutions directly in production. This shift gives designers massive leverage to scale their impact and shape the product. As Katarina puts it: “It’s never been easier to hop on and start contributing to code, even if you’re not technical.”

02

Try everything and keep moving

With so many AI tools available, which ones are worth learning? Katarina’s advice is simple: try everything. No one has years of experience working this way yet. A designer with fifteen years of experience is figuring this out alongside someone who graduated last spring. “You will make quantum leaps if you take the time to actually learn these new tools,” she says. It’s also reflective of how Shopify operates: questioning existing processes and being willing to rethink how work gets done. But Katarina also cautions against losing sight of the problem you’re trying to solve and the people you’re building for by over-focusing on AI, especially when the conversation around what’s new vs outdated seems to change by the day.

03

Growth happens through real work

One of the defining moments in Katarina’s career came during a 2012 internship at Facebook. Despite having little experience designing software, she found herself in critiques alongside some of the industry’s best designers. "That three-month internship changed the entire trajectory of my career,” she says. “I credit that experience so much with where I am today and I'm in a position now where I can hopefully extend the same kind of opportunity.”

Enter: Shopify’s Design Apprenticeship Program (DAP). The six-month program embeds a small group of junior designers on product and brand design teams, where they’re paired with mentors and work on real, shipped products. Its driving philosophy is that designers grow fastest when they’re surrounded by experienced designers and trusted with meaningful work.

in action

Creating a vision that's hard to ignore

When Luke Dupont came back from the holidays in January, he noticed that everyone around him was building. “I got really scared because I wasn’t,” he says. “I was still just doing the thing that I’m really good at, which is Figma.” So he took the opportunity to dive in.

His demo revisits an idea he first explored months earlier: rethinking how a merchant’s online store could be built inside Shop. The first version was a Figma prototype, but it never went far. “It felt very static and very not real,” he says.

This time, he went straight to a coded prototype. In an afternoon, he built a working version using real merchant data and Shop's existing components: a store where every section could be rearranged, rebuilt for different shoppers, or generated from a prompt. Instead of turning it into a deck, he shared the prototype through a Quick link, so anyone could open it and watch it change as he worked. The link went up the chain. By Monday, Luke had a team and a real project.

I’ve been having more fun in my career than I have in years. Just having this new way to fully unlock and to build the thing, not just draw it.

Luke Dupont

Principal Product Designer, Shopify

Designers in Shopify's newly opened New York City office

in action

Meeting engineering more than halfway

Across Shopify, designers are getting closer to code. Design Apprentices Pearl Sequeira and Taylor Cottrell are two strong examples.

Pearl recently redesigned how the Shop app collects and displays buyer reviews. She started her exploration in Figma, then built the experience inside the app using Claude Code and Codex. “It helps us make decisions really fast, cut things that don't work, and double down on things that are beginning to look good,” she says. While she still uses Figma to map out a direction, she now turns to code to test the motion and interactions that are difficult to communicate with a static mock.

Taylor approached a similar problem from the other direction. Before opening Figma to design a new feed card, he dropped an old engineering spec into an AI assistant to quickly map out the technical constraints. The tool surfaced details like latency, lazy loading, and deduplication before he drew a single screen. Because of this groundwork, his subsequent conversations with engineers started from a shared understanding.

Engineers felt that I had gone more than halfway across the table to understand what they were dealing with. It made them more open to the stuff we ended up presenting.

Taylor Cottrell

Design Apprentice, Shopify

Design Apprentice Pearl Sequeira with Senior Staff Product Designer Staci Kelly in the NYC Design Studio

in action

One character, six tools

For much of her career, the things motion designer Yaël Bienenstock pushed for “would often just get watered down more and more as we got to the end of the project.” Motion was often the last thing on the timeline, squeezed into the nice-to-have category. Now, she can build them herself.

Her demo features a floating character she created for the design team's website, whose jacket transforms with every click. She modeled the character after a colleague using Krea, then jumped from tool to tool for the rest: Midjourney for the outfits, Gemini to fine-tune them, Rive for pinpoint edits on specific details, stills stitched into generated video, composited and timed in After Effects, then into Claude in the terminal for a working prototype an engineer could take to the finish line.

That creative freedom goes beyond work. With thousands of outfit photos in her camera roll, but no easy way to find them, Yaël built an app in her free time that turns mirror selfies into 3D avatars for cataloging her outfits, complete with animated icons and shaders.

You might not have a perfect output, and that's totally fine. Knowing that this is not where it ends—that was a huge unlock for me.

Yaël Bienenstock

Staff Motion Designer, Shopify
